items.definition: A REC is a separately tradable certificate proving that one megawatt-hour of electricity was generated by an eligible renewable resource and injected into a power grid; because electricity on a grid can't be traced back to its source once delivered, RECs exist as an electronic accounting mechanism to track and trade the 'renewable' attribute apart from the physical power itself.
items.core_idea: RECs decouple the claim of having used renewable energy from the physical electricity, allowing that environmental attribute to be created, traded, and sold independently of the underlying power delivery.
key_points: One REC certifies 1 MWh of generation from an eligible renewable source delivered to a grid
RECs exist primarily as electronic records, not physical goods
Trading/transfer of a REC happens separately from the electricity transaction
RECs exist because grid electrons can't be physically distinguished by generation source
relationships: REC markets primarily coexist with deregulated power markets
In regulated (monopoly utility) markets, renewable obligations are typically met via PPAs with renewable generators instead of REC purchases
trading_implications: A REC's value comes entirely from external compliance or voluntary demand, not from any physical energy property
common_misunderstandings: A REC is not the electricity itself — an owner can hold the renewable claim without ever physically receiving power from that generator

items.definition: Green energy is electricity produced from renewable sources such as solar, wind, tidal, or geothermal generation. Brown energy is electricity produced from conventional sources such as fossil fuels or nuclear generation; hydropower is often classified as brown power in many regions.
items.core_idea: These terms are the base vocabulary distinguishing renewable from conventional generation, used throughout REC and RPS discussions.
key_points: Green energy sources: primarily solar and wind, also tidal and geothermal
Brown energy sources: fossil fuels and nuclear generation
Hydropower is frequently categorized as brown power despite not being a fossil fuel
relationships: RPS rules define exactly which generation sources qualify as green/eligible for REC creation
common_misunderstandings: Hydropower is not automatically treated as green in many regulatory schemes

items.topic: REC price sensitivity to supply and demand
items.definition: Because RECs carry no intrinsic value, their price is driven entirely by the balance between regulator-mandated purchase requirements and available supply. When eligible supply is short relative to the requirement, prices rise toward the alternative compliance payment (the regulatory penalty for non-compliance) and stay elevated as long as the shortage persists; when supply exceeds the requirement, prices collapse toward zero as excess holders compete just to sell.
items.core_idea: REC prices behave as a bounded market between zero and the compliance penalty price, governed by quota supply/demand rather than production cost or physical commodity fundamentals.
key_points: The alternative compliance payment acts as an effective price ceiling
Sustained shortage keeps prices near the penalty price
Oversupply drives prices toward zero (example: 10 million RECs created but only 2 million required leads sellers to bid near zero)

RECs and similar environmental products generally: have no inherent value, derive demand purely from regulatory compliance needs, are highly sensitive to supply/demand shifts, and are only usable within the specific jurisdiction of the regulator that created the requirement
relationships: Interacts directly with RPS-set purchase requirements and the alternative compliance payment penalty level
trading_implications: REC price risk is primarily regulatory/quota risk, not fuel-cost or weather-driven risk
Traders need to track eligible generation supply against the mandated requirement rather than production economics
common_misunderstandings: REC prices are not anchored to generation cost — a REC can trade near zero even if the underlying generation was costly, if supply overshoots the mandate

items.topic: Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) and REC product segmentation
items.definition: An RPS is typically a state-level (in the US) regulation requiring that a specified share of consumed power come from renewable generation, along with eligibility criteria such as generator location, generation technology, and generation date. Because these criteria can be layered (e.g. technology type combined with in-state/out-of-state origin), a single RPS can give rise to several distinct, non-fungible traded REC products.
items.core_idea: The specific design of an RPS determines how many separate REC product types exist in a market, since RECs satisfying different eligibility criteria are not interchangeable.
key_points: RPS mandates a minimum renewable share of consumption, set at the state level in the US
Common eligibility criteria: generator location, generation technology, generation date

Example: an RPS requiring 10% renewable power, with half from solar PV, and half of each category from in-state facilities, creates four distinct products — in-state solar, in-state non-solar, out-of-state solar, out-of-state non-solar RECs
relationships: Drives REC naming conventions, e.g. a New Jersey solar REC (NJ SREC) meets New Jersey's solar-specific requirement
trading_implications: Traders must track each jurisdiction's specific RPS carve-outs since RECs meeting different criteria are not fungible substitutes for each other
common_misunderstandings: A REC is not one uniform national product — an SREC from one state's program generally cannot satisfy a non-solar or out-of-state requirement elsewhere

items.topic: REC registration and ownership transfer via registries
items.definition: Generators register renewable production with a registry, which cross-checks the claimed generation against actual power grid injection records to verify it. Once a REC is created, ownership transfer on a trade is simply an electronic change of owner-of-record in the registry.
items.core_idea: The registry is the trust and audit mechanism that ties REC issuance to verified physical generation, preventing double-counting or fabricated certificates.
key_points: Generators register production with a registry to have RECs created
The registry cross-checks generation claims against the power grid
Ownership transfer on trade is an electronic record change, with no physical delivery involved
relationships: Underpins the integrity of REC trading described elsewhere in the chapter

items.definition: Vintage is the calendar year in which a REC's underlying generation occurred. RPS rules typically restrict how long after its vintage year a REC can still be used to satisfy compliance obligations — the source gives an example of a three-year usability window.
items.core_idea: Vintage functions like a shelf life or expiration window governing how long a REC remains eligible for compliance use.
key_points: Vintage = the year the REC's underlying generation took place
RPS programs typically define a maximum eligibility age for compliance use (example given: within three years of generation)
